entry.title:
Some observations about the "total" automation of software engineering:
1. There are more software ...
entry.summary: Continuing the conversation from yesterday's Social posts, Francois Chollet argues that despite agents now writing roughly 100% of code, software engineering has not been 'totally automated': there are more engineers than in 2025, they work harder than ever, and company bottom lines are not improving from AI adoption. He concludes that automation must be analyzed at the systems level, since automating one aspect simply shifts bottlenecks and creates new friction elsewhere.

entry.title: Social Summary: October 17, 2026
entry.summary:
Recursive AI development dominated discussion. Anthropic's Claude Devs reported Claude now writes ~90% of Claude Code with merged PRs doubling since June, and Boris Cherny credited Claude Code Review with catching nearly every bug — together signaling an AI self-improvement loop.

  • Policy and sovereignty ran hot: Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch urged Europe not to cede frontier AI to the US and China (317k views); Anthropic reportedly drafted frontier-AI regulation with lawmakers; Nathan Lambert flagged China's signal on ending larger open models.
  • Open-source momentum: Jim Fan released the ASPIRE robotics framework; Perplexity open-sourced Decision Models; Artificial Analysis ranked Reflection's Beam among US open-weights leaders and crowned Liquid AI's d1-ultra on its Decision Index.
  • Hardware economics: vLLM's benchmark showing AMD MI355X beating NVIDIA B300 by 24% on Kimi K3 serving sparked infrastructure debate.

Overall sentiment: excitement about agentic and self-improving AI capabilities, mixed with growing policy anxiety in Europe, the US, and China.

entry.title:
Should Europe leave frontier AI to the Americans and the Chinese?
The idea has gained ground in Eur...
entry.summary: Arthur Mensch argues that the idea of Europe ceding frontier AI to the US and China, which is gaining ground in Europe, is a fundamental mistake, urging that Europe must build its own frontier capability while the choice remains open, linking to a full article.

entry.title:
Claude writes about 90% of Claude Code's code.
From June to September, merged PRs more than doubled...
entry.summary: Anthropic's Claude Devs account reports that roughly 90 percent of Claude Code's codebase is now written by Claude itself. From June to September, merged PRs more than doubled while the revert rate fell by over 40 percent, and the team published details on the code review process changes that enabled this.

entry.title: String theory is what happens when an intelligent system is starved of sensory input and starts hall...
entry.summary: Chollet argues string theory exemplifies what happens when an intelligent system is starved of sensory input and begins hallucinating, concluding that intelligence requires grounding, that intelligence itself is rarely the bottleneck for solving impactful problems, and that the true bottleneck is iterated contact with reality.

entry.title: SSMs had the nice asymptotics but kept missing out on the inference goodies Transformers get for fre...
entry.summary: Following yesterday's Research on ReplaySSM, Tri Dao shares the broader lesson, Tri Dao reflects that SSMs' failure to benefit from inference optimizations like speculative decoding and quantization was due to caching the wrong things, arguing that the same IO-aware memory principle behind FlashAttention, Mamba scan, and paged KV caching explains the biggest wins, which came from taking memory IO seriously rather than new architectures.

entry.title: Meta has released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, achieving Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index...
entry.summary: Artificial Analysis's headline post on Meta's Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full models (GA September 2026), which score 52 and 56 on Intelligence Index v4.3 versus 48 for Muse Spark 1.3, with the largest gains on agentic benchmarks like Terminal-Bench 4.0 (+24 points). Wonder is on Meta's first-party API; Wonder Full is limited to Muse Code users.

entry.title: Social Summary: October 12, 2026
entry.summary:
Community discussion split between a viral builder thesis and substantive research news. Andrej Karpathy topped the day by reviving his point that public understanding of LLM capability is sharply stratified, resonating with Ethan Mollick's observations that even lab insiders underuse frontier models and that human-AI 'cyborgs' are rapidly taking over math research.

  • @levelsio dominated engagement volume with his 'software is dead' / personal-software thesis (9 related posts), arguing normies already build ephemeral tools inside AI chats — sparking both strong agreement and backlash over job displacement
  • Sakana AI's @hardmaru announced the MASS paper on recursive self-improvement via multi-agent self-supervision, drawing serious research attention
  • Clement Delangue open-sourced RL environments built from OpenAI's math problems, praised as concrete ecosystem infrastructure
  • Jerry Liu (LlamaIndex) offered a technically deep take on models bootstrapping their own ground-truth training data, plus a hands-on OCR model review
  • Yann LeCun sketched a generalization-theory framing for self-supervised learning; LangChain's @hwchase17 laid out an agent architecture vision and posed open questions on enterprise agent identity
  • Contrarian economic analysis from The Economist's Callum Williams (via @MTSlive) argued AI is delivering near-zero bottom-line gains, tempering builder optimism
  • A take endorsing Terence Tao's view that superintelligence must remain interpretable generated thoughtful philosophical discussion

entry.title: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *wid...
entry.summary: Karpathy revives an earlier observation that public understanding of LLM capability is sharply stratified: roughly 6B people have barely touched LLMs, 1-2B are casual users who see them as improved search or writing aids, and only about 20M people (0.2%) use frontier-grade models professionally in math and code. He argues this perception gap is widening into a funnel rather than a simple disagreement between two camps.

entry.title: Social Summary: October 11, 2026
entry.summary:
Intelligence explosion skepticism dominated the day's discussion. Ramez Naam's interview thread series argued the AI self-improvement loop is 5-10x too weak for takeoff, citing OpenAI's own token/researcher figures, rapid plateaus when scaling Claude Opus 5.5 agent swarms, and gaps between Anthropic's system cards and leadership rhetoric.

  • Francois Chollet delivered the conceptual highlight: the field's shift from transductive token completion to inductive, on-the-fly reasoning-chain synthesis
  • Yann LeCun clarified his critique targets autoregressive discrete-token prediction specifically, not AI broadly
  • Nathan Lambert flagged low net data quality as a reward-hacking amplifier and reported a ~30% drop in top open-model HuggingFace downloads, prompting a metrics rebuttal from HF CEO Clement Delangue
  • Practitioner threads from Boris Cherny and LangChain's Harrison Chase emphasized orchestration efficiency: routing cut Open SWE costs 64%, and many agent steps are yes/no calls rather than generation
  • Naam showed intellectual honesty by self-rebutting on OpenAI's claimed math breakthrough, while Ethan Mollick captured the OpenAI-vs-Anthropic cultural moment via a mathematician's Opus 5.5 music video

Overall sentiment: empirically grounded and practitioner-focused, with the community favoring falsifiable claims over accelerationist hype.

entry.title: FULL INTERVIEW: Ramez Naam says AI's self-improvement loop is 5 to 10 times too weak to take off on ...
